title: India Approves Its First Dengue Vaccine, Qdenga, Ahead of 2027 Launch
excerpt: The DCGI has authorised Takeda's two-dose vaccine for ages 4 to 60, with no screening or prior infection needed — while India's own single-dose candidate DengiAll works through Phase III trials.
body:
• India's drug regulator, the DCGI, has granted market authorisation to Takeda's Qdenga — the first dengue vaccine approved in India — for people aged 4 to 60.
  • Qdenga is given in two doses three months apart, covers all four dengue serotypes, and needs no pre-vaccination screening or prior dengue infection.
  • Takeda expects to launch it in India in the first half of 2027; pricing has not been finalised.
  • Separately, India's indigenous single-dose candidate DengiAll, from Panacea Biotec and the ICMR, is in Phase III trials with more than 13,000 volunteers — for diaspora families, dengue protection for India trips is becoming a realistic 2027 conversation with a doctor.

India has approved its first dengue vaccine. The Drug Controller General of India has granted market authorisation, under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, to Takeda's Qdenga for individuals aged 4 to 60, the company said — a milestone for a disease that, on a modelling study published in Nature cited by Takeda, accounts for nearly 34 percent of the global burden in India, the highest share of any country.

"It has been approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed worldwide."

What was approved, and how it is given

Qdenga is a two-dose vaccine, with the doses given three months apart, designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes — all four of which circulate in India. Its practical advantage is who can receive it: unlike an earlier internationally available dengue vaccine, Qdenga can be given regardless of whether a person has previously been infected with dengue, and it does not require pre-vaccination screening. That distinction is the shadow that has hung over dengue vaccination for a decade — the earlier vaccine's restriction to people with a prior infection made programmes complicated and controversial; regulators have treated Qdenga's profile differently.

The Indian approval rests on a Phase III trial in Indian participants aged 4 to 60, which found the vaccine safe, well tolerated and capable of generating an immune response, Takeda said. The vaccine also holds World Health Organization prequalification and is recommended by the WHO for use in dengue-endemic regions without pre-vaccination screening. It has been approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed worldwide.

The burden it is aimed at

Takeda said reported dengue cases in India have risen 11-fold over the past two decades, with more than 1.13 lakh cases reported in 2025. Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, has no specific antiviral treatment, and can progress quickly to severe illness requiring hospitalisation. "All four dengue virus serotypes circulate in India, contributing to recurrent outbreaks," said Dr. Goh Choo Beng, Takeda's head of medical affairs for its Southeast Asia and India cluster.

Dr. Mahender Nayak, Takeda's head of intercontinental markets, said the company expects to launch the vaccine in India during the first half of 2027 and is working with regulators and other stakeholders on the rollout; pricing is yet to be finalised.

The homegrown candidate behind it

Qdenga is India's first approved dengue vaccine, but not its only shot at one. DengiAll, a single-dose tetravalent candidate developed by Panacea Biotec with the Indian Council of Medical Research, is in a Phase III trial across about 20 centres with more than 13,000 volunteers, in a randomised design where two participants receive the vaccine for every one who receives a placebo. ICMR Director General Dr. Rajiv Bahl has said the trial has completed almost a year of follow-up and researchers hope to unblind the study by the end of 2027 — putting a potential indigenous vaccine on a similar late-2027 horizon, if the data support approval.

For now, the actionable facts are the approval itself and the 2027 launch window. Families planning extended stays in India — including the diaspora's annual trips — should treat dengue vaccination as a question to raise with their doctor once Indian pricing and availability are announced, alongside the mosquito-protection basics that remain the first line of defence.
